requirements.statement: A discrete random variable takes countably many values and assigns positive probability to individual points via its probability mass function.

places.quote: A **Discrete Random Variable** $X$ is a [[Random Variable]] whose possible values form a finite or countably infinite set — typically a count, such as the number of claims — so its distribution is given by a [[Probability Mass Function (PMF)|probability mass function]] $p(x) = P(X = x)$.

requirements.statement: For a discrete random variable, P(N ≤ k) = P(N < k) + P(N = k), so including or excluding an endpoint changes the probability by the point mass there.

places.quote: **Endpoints matter.** $P(X \le 3)$ and $P(X < 3)$ differ by $p(3)$

requirements.statement: A continuous random variable has a density function f(x) and puts probability 0 on every single value, so P(X = a) = 0 and inclusion of endpoints does not matter.

places.quote: $P(X = c) = 0$ for every $c$, so $P(a < X < b) = P(a \le X \le b) = F(b) - F(a)$. Strict and weak inequalities give the same answer — unlike a [[Discrete Random Variable]].

requirements.statement: A probability density function is not a probability: probabilities are areas under the density, and the density only needs to be nonnegative and integrate to 1, so it can exceed 1.

places.quote: A valid density has $f(x) \ge 0$ and $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx = 1$. It is a *rate*, not a probability, so it can exceed 1: $\text{Uniform}(0, 0.5)$ has $f(x) = 2$.

requirements.statement: A uniform distribution on (a, b) has constant density 1/(b − a), which exceeds 1 when the interval length is less than 1.
